title: When the Experts Get It Wrong
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos reflects on her own hero worship of science-of-reading experts after reading Emina McLean's warning against following experts blindly. She uses the public exchange in which Kilpatrick, Ehri, Brady, Beck and Clemens agreed that advanced phonemic awareness needed more research as a model of healthy expert humility. The worry is how often tentative findings reach classrooms as certainties, and she cites an Equipped for Reading Success recommendation that she found incompatible with reading research. Drawing on Carl Hendrick and Steve Dykstra, she argues that teachers' contextual expertise counts, that practitioners should know where the science ends and their judgment begins, and that experts and publishers alike need to respect uncertainty.
points: Experts often hold a narrow understanding while teachers have a broad one, so classroom judgment is a legitimate complement to research.
Open expert disagreement about advanced phonemic awareness is a healthy model, but the nuance often disappears before recommendations reach schools.
Even a trusted book can contain recommendations that contradict the research base, so teachers need enough knowledge to evaluate advice.
Teachers must distinguish informed experts from self-interested influencers and know where the science ends and their judgment begins.
quotes: Unfortunately, full transparency from researcher to practitioner is too often lacking as demonstrated in Nicola Bell’s A Deep Dive into Phonemic Proficiency, which explores the same disputes about advanced phonemic awareness skills that Timothy Shanahan does but also covers more contested ground.
Isn’t this type of exchange exactly what we want from researchers, an acknowledgement of the unknown and a plan to know it?
You don’t know what the scientists know; but they don’t know what you know either.
Suffice it to say that the methods described are completely incompatible with what research has reliably revealed about effective reading instruction.

Above all, teachers need to know the difference between an informed expert and a self-interested influencer, while also acknowledging that experts can be so far removed from the classroom that they may get the research right but the recommendation wrong.
Let’s resign our heroes to Homeric legend and reassign a shared burden for decision-making in the school setting.
